newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Californians take new aim at local taxes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Californians take new aim at local taxes.

text.p: The activists who led California's anti-tax revolt in the 1970s will try soon to complete the job with an initiative seeking to require that all local taxes be submitted for voter approval.

If the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is successful on election day on November 5, many local governments in the state will face a profound change in funding that could alter California's political landscape.

Known as the Right to Vote on Taxes Act, Proposition 218 being put to voters as part of a much wide national and local ballot, has attracted little public attention when compared to more explosive state initiatives, such as a proposal to ban state and local government affirmative action programmes.
Polls indicate voters are evenly divided on the tax measure which has shaken elected officials in California and municipal analysts on Wall Street.

"In terms of the general population, this (Proposition 218) is the one that is most likely to affect the most people," said David Brodsly, a vice president at Moody's Investors Service, a leading U.S. credit rating agency.
MEASURE WOULD MAKE CASH RAISING HARDER

The measure would make it more difficult for counties and other local governments to raise fees, assessments and taxes. Already at the bottom of the political "food chain", California counties and other local governments could lose precious revenues and be forced to slash services, officials say.

"This measure not only endangers our long-term fiscal solvency," said Zev Yaroslavsky, Los Angeles County Supervisor. "More importantly, it poses a mortal danger to some of our most basic services such as sheriff's patrols and fire suppression, not to mention park and library operations."
Beyond its impact on local government finances, the initiative could shift power to the state and change the way local elected officials make decisions, commentators said.

"The foundation of our democracy was "No taxation without representation,' not "No taxation without a vote,'" said Dan Wall, deputy director of the California State Association of Counties, a lobbying and education group. "This one little proposition transforms a representative democracy into a direct democracy, where decision making can't happen in any effective fashion at the local level."
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association insists that opponents of the measure are trying to scare voters by overstating its implications.
"The sky will not fall. The world will not end. Civilisation will not perish," the association said in a campaign leaflet.
CONCERNS ON WALL STREET
Though most Californians know little about the proposition, it has attracted the attention of the public finance community in California and on Wall Street.

Bob Giroux, vice president at Nelson Communications, which is coordinating the campaign to defeat Proposition 218, said municipal bond underwriters, bond counsel and other professionals have joined it.
"Word is spreading out across the municipal finance industry," Giroux said. "They have a legitimate concern with the potential impact of the initiative."

The California Public Securities Association is a member of the campaign committee working to defeat the proposition. Underwriter Stone & Youngberg has urged its clients to vote against it, warning of the "devastating effect the initiative will immediately have on local government finance."
The California Society of Municipal Analysts has said the measure could have negative credit implications for some local government bond issues.
ASSOCIATION SAYS OPPONENTS EXAGGERATE IMPLICATIONS

Jonathan Coupal, who helped to draft Proposition 218 for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said bond firms were exaggerating its negative implications because they "make tens of millions of dollars off California debt".

"The alleged impact that (proposition) 218 is going to have on local government finance is being grossly overstated," said Coupal, who is director of legal affairs for the association. "The world won't come to an end. It won't."

Though California state treasurer Matt Fong has not taken a position on Proposition 218, he has accused opponents of the tax initiative of overstating claims that the bond market would be adversely affected by its passage.
"It's wrong for people to say the market will come crashing down or that bondholders will not be paid if proposition 218 is passed," Fong said.
PROPOSITION DESIGNED TO CLOSE LOOPHOLES
Proposition 218 was designed to close loopholes in California's Proposition 13, which was also led by activists from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

The passage in 1978 of Proposition 13 rolled back local property taxes and drastically curtailed the ability of counties to raise revenues to cover expenses. It also set off a wave of tax reduction efforts across the country.

During the boom years of the 1980s, California's counties were able to provide for services. But in the recession of the early 1990s, property tax growth rates diminished at the same time the cost of providing services increased.

Adding to the pressure, the California state Legislature began shifting billions of dollars in property tax revenues away from counties to the state's cash-strapped school system and increasing other mandates.

"Working for a county since 1978 has been an experience in increasing financial crisis management," said Larry Monteilh, Los Angeles County's treasurer-tax collector. With limits on property taxes due to Proposition 13 and constraints on other revenues, "counties struggle on a knife's edge of fiscal solvency," Monteilh said.

Despite these limits, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association said California politicians have created an end run around Proposition 13 by expanding the use of assessments and fees that were not put to voters for approval.
"Proposition 218 will essentially close all these loopholes," Coupal said.

Proposition 218, which would apply to all cities, counties, special districts, redevelopment agencies and school districts in the state, would strengthen existing law to require that all new local taxes be submitted to voters for approval. It would also allow property owners to approve new assessments and strictly limit the use of fees and charges.
Municipal analysts said local governments may be required to reduce or repeal some existing property-related fees and assessments that do not meet the measure's restrictions.
One analyst has estimated that the measure would reduce local revenues by about $100 million per year. Opponents insist the amount would be significantly greater.
